sentences: In 1881, the doctor returns to the city after serving in a war abroad and starts looking for a place to live.
An old friend of his tells him that the detective is looking for someone to split the rent at a flat at an address in the city but cautions the doctor about the detective's eccentricities.
The detective and the doctor meet and, after assessing each other and the rooms, they move in.
The detective is a "consulting detective", and his frequent guests are clients.
After a demonstration of the detective's deductive skills, the doctor's disbelief turns into astonishment.
A telegram requests a consultation in a murder case.
The doctor accompanies the detective to the crime scene, an abandoned house on a city road.
Two inspectors are already on the scene.
The victim is a man from an American city, and documents found on his person reveal that he has a secretary.
The room is splashed in blood, and the word "RACHE" (German for "revenge") is written in it on one wall; however, the first victim's body shows no wounds.
Dismissing the message as a ploy to mislead the police, the detective deduces that the first victim was poisoned and supplies a description of the murderer.
Upon moving the first victim's body, they discover a woman's gold wedding ring.
The detective places notices in several newspapers about the ring and buys a facsimile of it, hoping to draw the murderer – who has apparently already tried to retrieve the ring – out of hiding.
An old woman answers the advertisement, claiming that the ring belongs to her daughter.
The detective gives her the duplicate and follows her, but she evades him in a way that leads the detective to believe that "she" was actually a young man in disguise, an accomplice to the murderer.
A day later, the first inspector visits the detective and the doctor, telling them that he has arrested a suspect.
He went to a landlady's boarding house where the first victim and the secretary stayed before the murder.
The first victim, a drunk, attempted to kiss the landlady's daughter, which caused their immediate eviction.
He, however, came back later that night and attempted to grab the daughter, prompting her older brother to attack him.
He attempted to chase the first victim with a cudgel but claimed to have lost sight of him.
The first inspector has him in custody on this circumstantial evidence.
The secretary is later found dead in his hotel room, stabbed through the heart and with the word "RACHE" written in blood on the wall.
The only things the secretary had with him were a novel, a pipe, a telegram saying "the avenger is in the continent", and a small box containing two pills.
The detective tests the pills on an old and sickly Scottish Terrier in residence at the flat.
The first pill produces no evident effect, but the second kills the terrier.
A young street urchin then arrives.
He is the leader of the street gang, a group of street children the detective employs to help him occasionally.
The urchin has summoned a cab the detective wanted.
The detective sends him down to fetch the cabby, claiming to need help with his luggage.
When the cabby comes upstairs, the detective handcuffs and restrains him.
The captive cabby is the avenger, the murderer of the first victim and the secretary.

In a valley in a western territory in 1847, the pioneer and a little girl, the only survivors of a small party of pioneers, are rescued from death by a party of church members led by the church leader, but only on the condition that they adopt and live under the church's faith.
Years later in 1860, the now-grown girl befriends and falls in love with the avenger.
However, the church leader forbids her from marrying outside the faith and demands that she marry either the secretary or the first victim, both sons of members of the church's ruling council.
The pioneer, who has adopted the girl and sworn never to marry his daughter to a church member, sends word to the avenger in order to help them escape.
The girl is given one month to choose between her suitors.
The avenger arrives on the eve of the last day, and they all escape under cover of darkness.

While the avenger is hunting in the mountains, the church members catch up to the escapees; the secretary kills the pioneer, while the girl is taken back to the church members' settlement and forced to marry the first victim.
She dies of a broken heart less than a month later.
The avenger breaks into the first victim's house the night before the girl's funeral to kiss her body and remove her wedding ring.
In 1888 the young woman arrives at the flat of the detective with a case.
She explains that, ten years earlier, her father the captain disappeared immediately after arriving in the city from his military service abroad.
The young woman contacted his friend, the major, who denied having seen him.
Four years later she received a valuable pearl in the post, a gift repeated every year for six years.
With the sixth pearl, she also received a letter asking for a meeting, claiming that she is a "wronged woman".
The detective takes the case and soon discovers that the major had died a week before the young woman received the first pearl.

The only further clue the young woman can give the detective is a map of a fortress found in her father's desk, appended with the words, "the mark of the four conspirators: the one-legged man, the first accomplice, the second accomplice, the third accomplice" and four small cross-like symbols.

Following the letter's instructions, the detective, the doctor and the young woman go to a theatre, where they meet a coachman who takes them to the house of the major's son, the anonymous sender of the pearls.
He reveals that the captain did, in fact, visit the major, demanding his half of a treasure that the major had secretly brought back from the colony.
In the ensuing quarrel, the captain suffered a heart attack and died, striking his head on the treasure box as he fell.
Afraid he would be suspected of murder, the major buried the body and hid the treasure, leaving out a small gold chaplet studded with twelve pearls.

The major's son and his twin brother only learned of this when their father revealed it while on his deathbed; he was about to reveal to them where the treasure was hidden, when a bearded man appeared at the window and the major died of fear.
The brothers tried and failed to catch the intruder and later on, found a note pinned to the major's body which read "the mark of the four conspirators".
The major's son began sending the young woman the pearls to make things right and the brothers searched for the treasure.
Six years later, the twin brother found and withheld it; the major's son then contacted the young woman so they could both confront the twin brother and demand their shares.
The party, now accompanied by the major's son, heads to the twin brother's house, a lodge in a suburb.
As they enter, the worried housekeeper reveals that the twin brother has locked himself in his laboratory and refuses to come out.

The young woman stays downstairs to comfort the housekeeper, while the others rush up to the laboratory; through the keyhole, they can see the twin brother slumped in his chair, with a "fixed and unnatural grin" upon his face.
The detective and the doctor break down the door, to discover the twin brother in a state of rigor mortis.
Upon further inspection of the body, the detective discovers a poisonous thorn above the twin brother's ear.
The treasure box is also gone, though there is a hole in the ceiling where it used to be.

While the police wrongly take the major's son in as a suspect, the detective deduces from footmarks and other clues that there are two persons involved in the murder: a one-legged white man, and a small Andamanese accomplice, who accidentally stepped in creosote.
Borrowing a trained scent hound from a naturalist, the detective traces the pair to a boat landing.
Learning that the one-legged man has hired a steam launch, the detective, with the help of his gang of street children and his own disguises, traces the boat to a repair yard.
In a police launch, the detective and the doctor pursue the steam launch when it flees the yard; the islander attempts to shoot a dart at the detective, but is shot dead himself.
The one-legged man attempts to flee, running the steam launch aground, but is captured.
However, the treasure box is now empty; the one-legged man, not wanting to surrender the gems, had scattered them into the river during the chase.
The one-legged man confesses that he was once a soldier of an infantry regiment in the colony, and lost his right leg to a crocodile while bathing in a river.
He then became an overseer on an indigo plantation, but when the 1857 rebellion occurred, was forced to flee to the fortress.

While standing guard one night, he was overpowered by Sikh troopers, who gave him a choice; be killed, or help them waylay a man who serves an outlawed rajah and is bringing his jewellery to the fortress for safekeeping.
The robbery and murder took place, but the crime was discovered, although the hidden jewels were not.
The one-legged man and his accomplices were convicted and sentenced to penal servitude, and were transferred after some time to a prison in a remote island group.
The one-legged man discovered that the major and the captain, who were guards at the convict barracks, had lost money playing cards.

The one-legged man made a deal with the officers, that the major would recover the treasure and in return send a boat to pick up the captain, the one-legged man and the Sikhs so they could all meet and divide it.
However, the major stole the treasure for himself, returning to his home country after inheriting a fortune from his uncle.
The captain went after the major but never returned and the one-legged man vowed vengeance against the major.
Four years later, the one-legged man escaped prison with the help of an islander whose life he had once saved.
It was the news of this escape that shocked the major into his fatal illness.
The one-legged man arrived too late to hear of the treasure's location, but left the note in the room anyway as revenge for the treatment of himself and the Sikhs.

When the twin brother eventually found the treasure, the one-legged man only planned to steal it; however, a miscommunication led the islander to kill the twin brother before the one-legged man could stop him.

In the city, 1889, the detective and the assistant are visited by a country doctor, asking for the aid of the detective, beginning by reading him a legend that has run in a noble family since the time of the civil war, when a wicked ancestor kidnapped a farmer's daughter.
When the girl escaped the wicked ancestor pursued her, swearing a curse upon himself in his mad rage.

The wicked ancestor's companions witnessed the girl dead of fear and the wicked ancestor killed by a demonic hound that is said to have haunted the moorland ever since, causing the premature death of many members of the family.

The country doctor further explains that his friend, the philanthropic baronet, who took the legend very seriously and had a weak heart, had resided at the family hall after amassing a fortune in a distant country.

When the baronet's body was found in a yew alley, with an expression of horror on his face, the death was attributed to cardiac arrest; however the country doctor had noticed large canine paw prints near the body.
The old baronet had been the eldest of three brothers of the family and the nephew, the Canadian son of the deceased second brother, is the old baronet's heir.
The rather vicious third brother died of yellow fever on another continent in 1876.
The country doctor, the executor of the old baronet's will, fears it might not be wise to bring the nephew to the moorland in light of the possible supernatural dangers.
Though the detective dismisses the legend as a fairy tale he meets the nephew when the new baronet arrives in the city.

It transpires that strange things are already happening to the nephew; one of his old boots has been stolen, he has received an anonymous letter warning him against the moor, and someone has been following him in a hansom.

The country doctor reveals that the nephew's inheritance is about £740,000; in view of these high stakes the detective asks the assistant to act as the nephew's bodyguard and to investigate things on the moorland.
Upon arriving in the moorland, the assistant, the country doctor and the nephew learn that a convict, a convicted murderer, has escaped from the nearby prison and is loose on the moor.
At the family hall they are introduced to the married butler and housekeeper.
The assistant sends detailed accounts of his investigations to the detective, particularly focusing on the local residents.
A neighbouring pair of siblings stand out; the neighbour is over-friendly, drops hints about the hound, and warns the assistant against attempting to cross the dangerous mire.
His sister, without his knowledge, repeatedly tries to get the nephew to flee back to the city.
Another neighbour is a perpetual busybody and troublemaker, including threatening to bring a lawsuit against the country doctor for excavating nearby barrows.
The nephew falls in love with the sister, though her brother strongly objects to the romance.
The butler repeatedly sends candlelight signals to someone on the moor.
Following the butler one night, the assistant and the nephew discover that the convict is the housekeeper's younger brother and that she and her husband have been leaving food out for him.
During an unsuccessful attempt to catch the convict the assistant sees a strange man standing on a tor.
The assistant and the nephew learn from the butler that the busybody's estranged daughter had once written to the old baronet.

After a failed attempt to interrogate the daughter, the assistant investigates the man on the tor and discovers that it is the detective, who has been investigating in secret to hide his direct involvement.

The detective reveals that the neighbour is the murderer, and the sister is actually his wife, abused and forced into posing as his sister; however, the detective does not have enough proof to convince the authorities.

The detective and the assistant fear they hear the nephew fleeing from a baying hound, and falling from a cliff; they find the dying man is the convict; the butler had given the convict the nephew's discarded clothes, and the neighbour's hound, having been set on the trail with the nephew's stolen boot, had confused the scent.
At the family hall, the detective reveals to the assistant that the portrait of the wicked ancestor bears a remarkable resemblance to the neighbour.
The detective decides to use the unwitting nephew as bait; he orders him to visit the neighbour that evening, and then walk across the moor on foot.
The detective and the assistant then pretend to leave for the city, but instead hide near the neighbour's house with a police inspector from the city police.
Despite thick fog, they manage to kill the hound (a hybrid of bloodhound and mastiff) when the neighbour unleashes it after the nephew.
They go to the neighbour's house to find he has bound his wife to a column and vanished into the mire, where he is presumed to have drowned.

After the nephew and the country doctor depart on a sea voyage, to repair the baronet's shattered nerves, the detective explains to the assistant that the neighbour was really a hidden heir, the secret son of the old baronet's youngest brother.

A physical and spiritual throwback to the wicked ancestor, the hidden heir had bought the black hound and painted it with phosphorus to make it look diabolical; either by fright or direct attack, he hoped the dog would remove all the other heirs so that he could inherit the family fortune.
He had promised the daughter to help her divorce her estranged husband and then marry her himself and thus perasuaded her to lure the old baronet out of his house on the night of the murder.
Intending to save the nephew, the sister had sent the anonymous letter to him to thwart her husband's further schemes.
The detective remarks that he considers the neighbour one of his most cunning adversaries.
The detective receives a cipher message from an informant, a pseudonymous double agent of the master criminal.
The detective deciphers the message as a warning of a nefarious plot against a man, a country gentleman residing at a manor house.
Some minutes later, the inspector arrives at the detective's flat with news that the gentleman was murdered the night before.
The inspector, the detective, and the doctor travel to the manor house to investigate.
The manor house is surrounded by a shallow moat, which the murderer appears to have crossed as they fled the crime scene.

After interviewing the friend, a frequent guest at the manor house who discovered the body, they agree that suicide is out of the question and that someone from outside the house committed the murder.
The friend explains that the gentleman married after arriving in the country five years earlier.
The friend believes a secret society of men pursued the gentleman, and that he retreated to rural parts of the country out of fear for his life.
The gentleman's wife said her husband mentioned something called "the dreaded valley".
The detective learns that the housekeeper heard a sound, as if of a door slamming, half an hour before the alarm; the detective believes that this sound was the fatal shot.
A local detective and the inspector track a bicycle found on the grounds of the house to an American staying at a guest house.
The American appears to be the murderer, but there is no sign of him.
The detective asks the inspector to write to the friend, telling him that the police intend to search the moat the next day.
That night, they lie in wait outside the manor house and see the friend fish the clothes of the missing American out of the moat.
The friend refuses to explain the situation.
At that moment, the gentleman appears, alive and well.
He hands the doctor a written account called "the dreaded valley", which explains why he feared for his life.
The gentleman explains that he had spotted an enemy of his in the area and expected an attack.
When the enemy attempted to shoot the gentleman in his study, the gentleman grabbed hold of the enemy's shotgun; in the struggle, the enemy was shot in the face.
With the friend's help, the gentleman dressed the man in his clothes to confuse his enemies.
He then hid himself in the old priest hole at the manor house.
The main narrative pauses to explain the gentleman's past in another country.
The gentleman's real name was a different one and he had been a private agency detective in a large city.

Working undercover for the detective agency, the agent had travelled to a mining valley (the titular dreaded valley) under an assumed name to infiltrate a corrupt coal miners' masonic lodge, secretly a cover for a murderous gang of protection racketeers.
After the agent brought the gang to justice, the surviving criminals attempted to kill him.
The agent changed his name to the gentleman's and fled to the country.
The detective urges the gentleman to leave the country.
The gentleman takes this advice, but, shortly after, the detective learns from the friend that the gentleman was lost overboard on the ship to another continent.
The detective believes the master criminal was responsible for ending the gentleman's life and he swears to bring the master criminal down.
The Grand Duke of a small duchy and hereditary King of a small kingdom visits the detective's flat.
Five years earlier, he had engaged in a secret relationship with an American opera singer.
He is set to marry a young Scandinavian princess, but worries that her family will call the marriage off should they learn of this impropriety.
The king seeks to regain a photograph of the singer and himself together which he gave to her as a token and which she now threatens to send to his fiancée's family.
The next day, the disguised detective visits the singer's neighbourhood, examines her home from outside, and learns of her lifestyle and daily routine from the local ostlers.
A lawyer visits the singer for half an hour, after which they leave separately and hurriedly for a particular church.
The detective follows them there and is unexpectedly asked to be a witness to their wedding.
Upon returning to the detective's flat, he enlists his friend to assist in a ploy that will reveal the location of the photograph.
The detective arranges for several men to start a fight outside the singer's home as she returns from her usual afternoon carriage ride, and fakes being injured in the scuffle.
Once he has been carried inside to recover, his friend throws in a smoke bomb and shouts that a fire has started.
In the confusion, the detective watches the singer's reactions and determines where she has hidden the photograph.
He notifes the king of these findings and arranges for the three to visit the singer the following morning so they can collect it.
When they arrive, they find that the singer and the lawyer have left the country and taken the photograph with them, leaving behind a note and a second picture of the singer alone.

She explains that she had been warned that the king would almost certainly send the detective to act on his behalf, and after the incident with the smoke bomb she realised what he'd done and followed the detective to the detective's flat to confirm his identity.
She assures the king that she and the lawyer are in love, and that the king need not fear any reprisals from her as long as he takes no action against the couple.
Even though the detective has failed to retrieve the photograph, the king believes the photograph to be safe because the singer is a woman of her word.
He offers an emerald ring as payment, but the detective declines in favor of the picture of the singer.

His friend concludes the story by noting that the case prompted the detective to stop mocking the cleverness of women, and that he always referred to the singer as "the woman" from that point on as a way of honoring and respecting her victory over him.
In another story, the detective shows his friend an amethyst-inlaid gold snuffbox the king sent for his service.
A man, a city pawnbroker, comes to consult the detective and the doctor.
While studying this prospective client, both the detective and the doctor notice his red hair.

The pawnbroker tells them that some weeks before, his young assistant urged him to respond to a newspaper advertisement by a league for red-headed men offering highly-paid work to only red-headed male applicants.
The next morning, the pawnbroker was hired to copy out an encyclopaedia for four hours each day at the league's office, at a salary of £4 per week.
The work was useless clerical labour, performed in nominal compliance with the will of an eccentric American millionaire who wanted to provide for the welfare of red-headed men like himself.
After eight weeks, the pawnbroker reported to the office, only to find a note on the door stating that the league had been dissolved.
He spoke with the landlord, who stated that he had never heard of the organisation.
The pawnbroker provides a description of the assistant, after which the detective and the doctor visit the pawnshop.
Concluding that a crime is about to be committed at a bank near the shop, the detective gathers the doctor, a police inspector from the city police, and the bank chairman that night.

As the four hide in the darkened bank vault, the bank chairman reveals that it holds a shipment of gold coins borrowed from a French bank; the detective suspects a wanted criminal of planning to steal them.
After more than an hour's wait, the criminal and his red-headed accomplice break upward through the vault floor.
The criminal is immediately apprehended, while the accomplice flees through the tunnel but is soon caught by police stationed at the shop.
Back at the detective's flat, the detective explains his reasoning to the doctor.
It was obvious to him from the start that the league had been devised with the sole intention of keeping the pawnbroker away from his pawnshop for a few hours every day.

According to the pawnbroker, the assistant pursued photography as a hobby and spent much of his time in the cellar under the excuse of developing the pictures, which made the detective think he might have been digging a passage to another building from there.

He had recognized the assistant as the criminal from the pawnbroker's description, and he saw during the pawnshop visit that the knees of the criminal's trousers were worn and dirty, confirming his suspicions about the digging.
Checking the buildings nearby, he determined that the bank was the only plausible target.

A young woman, a working-class girl who possesses a generous income as a result of a bequest from a relative, comes to the detective and the doctor for help after her fiancé disappears on their wedding day.

The fiancé, the detective learns, was a quiet and secretive man who wore a pair of tinted glasses, had a thick beard and moustache, and would not give the young woman his address, insisting that she leave letters at the local post office instead.
He would only meet her when her disapproving stepfather was out of the country on business.
The detective easily deduces that the stepfather and the fiancé are the same person.
The stepfather knew that he could only benefit from his stepdaughter's income while she remained unmarried, and so he hatched a plan to keep her single indefinitely.
As "the fiancé", he successfully sought her hand; he then engineered the fiancé's disappearance before the marriage could take place.
As he had hoped, the young woman remained loyal to her lost fiancé, saying she could never love another.
The detective confirms his theory by comparing the fiancé's letters to a missive from the stepfather.
Various small defects in the type indicate that they came from the same typewriter.
The stepfather boasts to the detective that he has broken no laws, but flees when the detective threatens to beat him with a riding crop.
The detective chooses not to divulge his findings to the young woman, knowing she will not believe him anyway.
He advises her to forget about the fiancé, though his words have little effect on her.
As for the stepfather, the detective predicts that his wicked ways will eventually lead him to the gallows.
A man, a widower and a major landowner who has a daughter, lives in a rural county with a fellow expatriate from a distant colony, a widower who has a son.
The fellow expatriate has been found dead near a woodland pool; it was reported that he was there to meet someone.
Two witnesses testify that they saw the fellow expatriate walking into the woods followed by the son, who was carrying a gun.

A girl, daughter of a lodgekeeper, says that she saw the two arguing and that, when the son raised his hand as if to hit his father, she ran to her mother; and while she was telling her mother what she saw, the son rushed to their house seeking help.
The girl and her mother followed the son back to the pool, where they found his father dead.
The son was arrested and charged with murder.
The daughter believes that the son is innocent and has contacted a police inspector, who in turn seeks help from the detective.
The son confirms the testimonies of the witnesses but explains that he was going into the woods to hunt, not to follow his father.
He later heard his father calling "Cooee" and found him standing by the pool, surprised to see him.
They argued heatedly, and the son decided to return to their farm.
Shortly after that he heard his father cry out and returned to find him lying on the ground.
The son insists that he tried to help him, but his father died in his arms.
The son refuses to give the cause of their argument, despite the coroner's warning that it could be damaging to his case if he does not reveal it.
The son also remembers that his father's last words were something about "a rat", but the son is uncertain of their meaning in the situation.
He also thinks he saw a cloak on the ground, which vanished while he was helping his father.
The daughter meets the detective, the inspector and the doctor in a hotel, and hopes that the detective has found a way to prove the son's innocence.
She also believes that she was the subject of the argument between the fellow expatriate and his son – the fellow expatriate wanted his son to marry her, but the son had refused.
The daughter had taken the son's side out of respect for him, and her father was also against the union.

The detective asks the daughter if he could meet her father, but she says his health worsened after the death of the fellow expatriate, whom he had known since they were in a region of the distant colony.
The detective decides to see the son.
The detective mistakenly surmises that the son knows who killed his father and is protecting someone.
It emerges that the daughter is right about the cause of the argument between the son and the fellow expatriate.
What she does not know is that the son actually loves her but could not follow his father's demand because he had married a barmaid before the daughter had returned from boarding school.
This burdened him, but he could not tell his father about his marriage because he would have been kicked out of the house and left unable to support himself.
When his wife heard of his troubles, however, she confessed that she was already married before they met, and therefore their marriage is invalid.
The detective, the doctor and the inspector go to the farm, and examine the fellow expatriate's and the son's boots.
They then head to the pool, following the track from the courtyard.
After examining the ground, the detective finds evidence of the presence of another man, besides the fellow expatriate and the son, whom he believes to be the murderer.

The detective deduces that the killer is left-handed (because the fellow expatriate was struck neatly on the left side of his head from behind, where a right-handed man would have struck him on the other side), and that the stranger is tall, has a limp and smokes cigars.
The inspector is not convinced.

At the hotel, the detective explains to the doctor that "Cooee" is an Australian cry and that the apparent reference to "a rat", overheard by the son, in fact comprised the last syllables of the name of a town, a place in the distant colony.
The person the fellow expatriate was meeting was, therefore, someone he knew from the distant colony.

The landowner, the daughter's father, then comes to their room (coincidentally being announced by a hotel employee right as the doctor is about to name him as the killer, after correctly interpreting the hints the detective has offered him), entering with a limp, and, realising that the detective has deduced the crime, confesses.
In his confession, the landowner explains that he was a member of a gang named after the town, a group of bushrangers in the distant colony.
They robbed a gold convoy in which the fellow expatriate was the wagon driver, and the landowner spared his life despite knowing that the fellow expatriate could later identify him.
The loot made the surviving gang members rich, and they moved to the home country.
Resolved to change, the landowner parted ways with his friends.
He bought land and got married, and then the daughter was born.
Some time later, the fellow expatriate tracked down the landowner and threatened to blackmail him unless he and his son were provided for.
In response, the landowner gave the fellow expatriate the farm and money, hoping this would satisfy him.
A young gentleman named the client visits the detective one night with a strange story.
His uncle the colonel had emigrated to the country overseas as a young man, establishing himself as a planter in a southern state and joining the rebel army, in which he rose to the rank of colonel.
In 1869 or 1870, he returned to the home country and purchased an estate near a town in a southern county, adopting a reclusive lifestyle.
He later allowed the client to live on the estate and gave him full access to the property, except for one storage room that was always kept locked.
On 10 March 1883, the colonel received a letter postmarked a distant port, bearing the inscription "the three letters" and containing only five orange pips.
The arrival of this letter badly unnerved the colonel, and he sent the client to bring a lawyer to the estate.
By the time the client returned, the colonel had retrieved a box marked "the three letters" from the locked room and burned its contents.
The colonel made a will naming his brother the father (the client's father) as his heir, with the intent that the client should eventually inherit the estate from him.
The colonel's already-reclusive behaviour became even more bizarre; he would either lock himself in his room and drink heavily, or rush about the grounds in a frenzy while carrying a pistol.
On 2 May 1883, seven weeks after receiving the letter, he was found dead in a garden pool.
The death was ruled a suicide, but the client did not believe that the colonel could have killed himself.
The father took possession of the estate and examined the room, finding scattered records of the colonel's time in the country overseas.
On 4 January 1885 he received a letter postmarked a northern port, identical to the one received by the colonel and containing instructions to put "the papers" on the sundial in the garden.
The client realised that the papers being demanded must have been the ones burned by the colonel.
Despite the client's urging, the father decided not to involve the police.
Three days later, he was found dead at the bottom of a chalk pit; the death was ruled an accident but again the client had his doubts.
The client has now received a letter postmarked the capital that orders him to put the papers on the sundial, but the local police are convinced that the letters are merely practical jokes.
The only clue he can provide is a page from the colonel's diary, dated March 1869 and detailing that pips were sent to three men; two were later "cleared" and one was "visited”.
The detective suggests that the client put the page in the box that had contained the other papers, along with a note detailing their destruction, and leave the box on the sundial.
After the client departs, the detective deduces that the colonel had returned to the home country and gone into hiding because something in the country overseas had prompted him to flee for his life.
The detective further concludes that the letters were sent from a sailing ship, based on their postmarks and the time lapse between the first two mailings and the recipients' deaths.

He recognises "the three letters" as the secret society, an anti-Reconstruction group in the southern region that was active until its sudden collapse in 1869 – triggered, the detective theorises, by the colonel's return to the home country with vital records that the other members have since been trying to recover.
Opponents of the secret society would receive a warning and would be killed unless they either fled or renounced their opposition.
The next morning's newspaper carries an article on the discovery of the client's body in the river, apparently the result of an accidental drowning after he had fallen off a bridge.

Now convinced that all three men of the client's family were murdered, the detective spends the day checking the records of sailing ships and finds only one that could have been in the distant port, the northern port and the capital when the letters were posted – an American barque, the suspect ship.

He puts five orange pips into an envelope with the note "the detective's initials for the client's initials", addresses it to the captain, and mails it to the vessel's home port of the port city, in another southern state.
He also sends a telegram to the port city's police informing them that the captain and mates – the only American crewmen – are wanted in the home country for murder.
The detective's desire for vengeance ultimately goes unfulfilled, as the suspect ship is destroyed in a severe gale.
No trace is ever found except for a broken sternpost marked "the ship's initials", seen floating on the waves of the ocean.
The story begins when a friend of the doctor's wife comes to the doctor's house, frantic because her husband, a family acquaintance, an opium addict, has gone missing.
The doctor helps her by pulling him out of the opium den and sending him home.
The doctor is surprised to find that the detective is there too, in disguise and trying to get information to solve a different case about a man who has disappeared.
The doctor stays to listen to the detective tell the story of the case of the businessman.
The businessman is a prosperous, respectable, punctual man.
His family's home is in the country, but he visits the city every day on business.
One day when the businessman was in the city, the businessman's wife also went to the city separately.
She happened to pass down a lane, a "vile alley" near the city docks, where the opium den is located.
Glancing up, she saw her husband at a second-floor window of the opium den.
He vanished from the window immediately, and the businessman's wife was sure that something was wrong.
She tried to enter the building, but her path was blocked by a lascar, who owns the opium den.
She fetched the police, but they did not find the businessman; the room behind the window was the lair of a dirty, disfigured beggar, known to the police as the vagrant.
The police were about to put her story down as a mistake of some kind when the businessman's wife noticed a box of wooden toy bricks that her husband said he would buy for their son.

A further search turned up some of the businessman's clothes; later, his coat, with the pockets stuffed with hundreds of pennies and halfpennies, was found on the bank of the river, just below the building's back window.
Bloodstains are found on the windowsill and bedroom floor.
The vagrant was arrested at once but would say nothing, except to deny any knowledge of the businessman, and also vehemently resisted any attempt to make him wash.
The detective was initially quite convinced that the businessman had been murdered, and that the vagrant was involved, so he investigated the den in disguise.

He and the doctor return to the businessman's home, to a surprise - it is several days after the disappearance, but on that day, the businessman's wife had received a letter from her husband in his own handwriting, with his signet ring enclosed, telling her not to worry.
This forces the detective to reconsider his conclusions, leading him eventually to an extraordinary solution.

The detective and the doctor go the police station where the vagrant is held; the detective brings a bath sponge, which he uses to wash the sleeping vagrant's dirty face and reveal him as the businessman.
The businessman has been living a double life, as a respectable businessman and as a squalid beggar.
In his youth, he had been an actor before becoming a newspaper reporter.

To research an article, he had disguised himself as a beggar for a short time, and was able to collect a surprising amount of money due to a skillset uncommon to beggars; his acting skills enabled him to emulate a more sympathetic character with make-up, as well as provide a repertoire of witty dialogue with which to entertain passers-by to offer coins — in this way, he was just as much a street performer as he was a beggar.
Some time later, he was saddled with a large unexpected debt, so he returned to the street to beg for several days to pay it off.
His newspaper salary was very small and, tempted by the much larger returns of begging, he eventually became a "professional" beggar.
His takings were large enough (averaging over £700 a year, ) that he was able to establish himself as a country gentleman, marry well, and begin a respectable family.
His wife and children never knew what he did for a living, and when he was arrested, he feared exposure more than prison or the gallows.
Since no murder has been committed, he is released, and the detective and the police agree to keep the businessman's secret on the condition that no more is heard of the vagrant.
